title: A MOTHER WAITED AT THE WINDOW FOR A SON WHO WOULD NEVER COME HOME.
paragraphs: A MOTHER WAITED AT THE WINDOW FOR A SON WHO WOULD NEVER COME HOME.

She thought her son was returning with victory, riches, and honor. She never imagined that the God he had defied had already ended his reign of terror. And the most disturbing part of this story isn't that a mother was waiting. It's what she was hoping her son would bring home.
“Through the window she looked forth, and cried, the mother of Sisera cried through the lattice, Why is his chariot so long in coming? Why tarry the wheels of his chariots?” — Judges 5:28, ASV
Somewhere in an ancient house, a mother stood beside a window.
Perhaps she had been there for hours.
Perhaps every distant sound made her turn her head.
The wheels of a passing cart. The footsteps of a servant. The faint noise of movement beyond the courtyard.
Was that him?
Was her son finally coming home?
She knew what his arrival should sound like.
The rumble of chariots. The pounding of horses. The unmistakable noise of a victorious commander returning from battle.
Her son was no ordinary soldier.
His name was Sisera.
He commanded nine hundred chariots of iron. He had military power, authority, and a reputation that made an entire nation tremble.
And somewhere behind all that power was a mother who still called him her son.
But that day, the road remained empty.
The chariots did not appear.
The familiar sound never came.
And what she did not know was that her son was already dead.
Not wounded.
Not delayed.
Not hiding somewhere until the danger passed.
Dead.
The man she expected to return in triumph had fled from the battlefield on foot. He had entered a woman's tent, believing he had found safety.
And there, his life had ended.
His mother kept looking toward the road.
But there was no son left to return.
And before we rush to feel sorry for her, Scripture asks us to look more closely.
Because what happened at that window reveals something deeply uncomfortable about the human heart.
Something about the things we celebrate.
The people we defend.
The evil we excuse when it benefits someone we love.
And the terrifying possibility of waiting confidently for a victory that God has already judged.
The story begins long before that mother appeared at the window.
Israel had once again done evil in the sight of the LORD.
Judges 4:1 tells us this plainly.
After the death of Ehud, the people returned to disobedience. And the LORD gave them over into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, whose military commander was Sisera.
For twenty years, Sisera's forces cruelly oppressed the Israelites.
Twenty years.
Think about that.
Children were born under oppression and grew up knowing nothing else.
Families lived beneath the shadow of military intimidation.
Generations learned what it meant to fear a powerful enemy.
Sisera had nine hundred iron chariots, according to Judges 4:3.
In that ancient world, such military equipment represented formidable power.
To frightened Israelites, those chariots may have seemed like an announcement that resistance was hopeless.
But there is something iron chariots cannot do.
They cannot overrule the God of Israel.
And there is something human power can never guarantee.
That the person who leaves home in the morning will return at night.
The Israelites cried out to the LORD.
And God raised up Deborah, a prophetess and judge in Israel.
Deborah summoned Barak and delivered the LORD's command to gather ten thousand men from Naphtali and Zebulun.
God promised to draw Sisera to the Kishon River and give him into Barak's hand.
Barak went to battle.
And Judges 4:15 records the turning point.
“And Jehovah discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots, and all his host, with the edge of the sword before Barak.” — ASV
The Hebrew verb translated “discomfited” is וַיָּהָם (vayyāhām), from the root המם (hāmam), meaning to throw into confusion, disturb, or rout.
The same God who seemed absent during twenty years of oppression was not powerless.
He had heard the cries of His people.
And the army that appeared unstoppable began to collapse.

Judges 5:20–21 poetically describes the heavens fighting and the torrent Kishon sweeping the enemy away. The song celebrates God's decisive intervention, although the narrative does not give us every physical detail of the battle.
Sisera abandoned his chariot.
Imagine that.
The commander whose power was represented by iron chariots was now running on his own feet.
The machinery that had inspired fear could not save him.
His military position could not protect him.
His reputation could not rescue him.
He fled to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite.
There was peace between Jabin's house and Heber's household, so Sisera had reason to believe he might be safe there.
Jael welcomed him inside.
He asked for water.
She gave him milk.
He lay down.
He asked her to stand guard.
And when he fell into a deep sleep, exhausted from his flight, Jael took a tent peg and a hammer and drove the peg through his temple.
Judges 4:21 records his death without disguising its violence.
The text does not present this as an ordinary model for Christians to imitate. It recounts a particular act within Israel's ancient deliverance from an oppressive military power.
And when Barak arrived searching for Sisera, Jael showed him the body.
The commander was dead.
His army was defeated.
Israel had been delivered.
But somewhere far away, a woman was still watching the road.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable.
Judges 5 is the victory song of Deborah and Barak.
It celebrates the LORD's triumph and recounts the courage, failure, and actions of different people during Israel's deliverance.
Near the end, the song suddenly changes scenes.
We are no longer standing beside the battlefield.
We are looking through a window.
The Hebrew of Judges 5:28 begins:
בְּעַד הַחַלּוֹן נִשְׁקְפָה וַתְּיַבֵּב אֵם סִיסְרָא
Beʿad haḥallôn nishqefāh vatteyabbēb ʾēm Sîserāʾ.
A close rendering is:
“Through the window she looked out and cried out, the mother of Sisera.”
The verb וַתְּיַבֵּב (vatteyabbēb) comes from the Hebrew root יבב (y-b-b), associated with crying out or wailing.
This is not merely a passing glance through a window.
The poetry depicts a woman looking outward and voicing her distress.
And then she asks:
מַדּוּעַ בֹּשֵׁשׁ רִכְבּוֹ לָבוֹא
Madduaʿ bōshēsh rikhbô lābôʾ?
“Why is his chariot so long in coming?”
Notice what she asks.
Not, “Is my son alive?”
Not, “Has something terrible happened?”
Her first recorded question concerns the delay of his chariot.
She is expecting the familiar signs of military success.
And the women around her offer an explanation.
They tell her that the soldiers must be dividing the spoils of victory.
Then comes one of the most chilling verses in the book of Judges.
Judges 5:30, in the American Standard Version, reads in part:
“Have they not found, have they not divided the spoil? A damsel, two damsels to every man.”
The Hebrew expression is even more disturbing:
רַחַם רַחֲמָתַיִם לְרֹאשׁ גֶּבֶר
Raḥam raḥămātayim lerōʾsh gever.
The word רַחַם (raḥam) literally means “womb.”
In this context, it is used as a degrading reference to female captives, counted as spoils for victorious men.
Some translations soften the wording into “a girl or two,” while others more directly convey its brutal implications.

The Hebrew wording does not explicitly describe every act the soldiers would commit, but its treatment of women as war booty is unmistakable. The context strongly evokes the sexual exploitation and enslavement associated with ancient warfare.
And suddenly the scene at the window changes.
This is not simply a grieving mother wondering why her son has not returned.
This is a household imagining that the delay is caused by the distribution of plunder, including captive women.
While one mother waits for her son, other mothers may be mourning children taken by war.
While she imagines embroidered garments, others face the loss of their homes, their freedom, and their dignity.
The poem places those expectations in front of us deliberately.
It exposes the moral blindness of people who benefit from oppression.
We must be careful here.
Scripture does not tell us everything Sisera's mother knew, every thought she had, or every action she personally approved.
The song is poetry, not a transcript of a private conversation. It portrays the expectations of Sisera's household through a scene of devastating irony.
But the irony is unmistakable.
They imagine victory.
God has already brought defeat.
They imagine captives.
Their commander has already fallen.
They imagine riches.
He will not return to enjoy them.
They imagine a celebration.
But the road will remain empty.
And this is the question that reaches across thousands of years and confronts us today.
What if some of the things we call blessings are actually things God is calling us to repent of?
What if we have become so accustomed to benefiting from something that we no longer ask whether it is righteous?
What if we defend wrongdoing because the person responsible is someone we love?
A son.
A daughter.
A spouse.
A friend.
A respected leader.
A person whose success makes us feel successful.
We know how easily love can become an excuse for silence.
We know what it is to say, “But you don't understand. He's a good person.”
Or, “She didn't mean it that way.”
Or, “Everyone does it.”
Or, “At least he's providing for his family.”
But provision does not sanctify exploitation.
Success does not erase injustice.
And love does not require us to call evil good.
Isaiah 5:20 warns:
“Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil.” — ASV
That warning does not belong only to ancient kings and commanders.
It belongs to every generation tempted to trade truth for comfort.
It belongs to parents who refuse to confront cruelty in their children.
It belongs to religious communities that protect reputation at the expense of victims.
It belongs to anyone who has mistaken worldly success for divine approval.
And it belongs to us whenever we become more concerned about whether someone we love gets caught than whether they turn from their sin.
That is a hard truth.
Because some of us have stood at our own windows.
Not literal windows, perhaps.
But places of waiting.
Waiting for someone to change.
Waiting for an apology that never came.
Waiting for a family member to return to God.
Waiting for a prodigal son or daughter to walk back through the door.
Waiting for a phone call.
Waiting for reconciliation.
Waiting for news that would make the pain finally stop.
And this is where we need to make an important distinction.
Not every mother waiting at a window is like Sisera's mother.
Some are praying for children trapped in addiction.
Some are waiting for sons serving in dangerous places.
Some have buried children and would give anything to hear their footsteps again.
Some are grieving relationships broken by betrayal, distance, or death.
Their tears are not condemned by this passage.
The Bible does not mock a mother's grief.
And we should never use this story to tell someone that their loved one's death was a punishment from God.
Judges describes a particular act of judgment within a particular moment in redemptive history. It does not give us permission to interpret every tragedy as evidence of someone's secret wickedness.

Jesus Himself rejected that kind of simplistic reasoning in Luke 13:1–5, calling everyone to repentance rather than allowing His listeners to assume that victims of tragedy were worse sinners than others.
The point of Sisera's mother's window is not that grief is shameful.
It is that human expectations can be tragically separated from God's truth.
And that should make every one of us examine our hearts.
Because the most dangerous kind of blindness is not always the blindness of someone who knows they are doing evil.
Sometimes it is the blindness of someone who has learned to celebrate it.
Someone who has grown comfortable with it.
Someone who has found a way to make it sound respectable.
Someone who has wrapped it in family loyalty, religious language, or personal ambition.
And the longer we do that, the harder repentance becomes.
But here is where the Gospel brings a hope that the window of Sisera's mother cannot provide.
There is another biblical story about a parent waiting for a son.
And the contrast is breathtaking.
In Luke 15, Jesus tells the parable of a younger son who demanded his inheritance, left his father's house, and wasted his possessions in reckless living.
He fell into poverty.
He became hungry.
He found himself longing for the food given to pigs.
And finally, Scripture says he came to himself.
He recognized his sin.
He decided to return home.
Not with excuses.
Not with a speech about how everyone had misunderstood him.
Not demanding that his father celebrate his choices.
He returned prepared to confess:
“Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight.” — Luke 15:21, ASV
And while he was still far away, his father saw him.
The father ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
The father did not call the son's rebellion righteous.
He did not pretend the wasted years had never happened.
But he welcomed the repentant son with extraordinary mercy.
The father said:
“For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.” — Luke 15:24, ASV
Do you see the contrast?
Sisera's mother expected a victorious son who had not returned.
The father in Jesus' parable welcomed a ruined son who had finally come home in repentance.
One household imagined the spoils of domination.
The other celebrated the restoration of a sinner.
One scene ends with the silence of a road.
The other ends with the sound of a feast.
And between those two scenes stands one of the greatest questions you will ever face.
Are you waiting for God to bless the life you refuse to surrender, or are you ready to come home to Him?
Maybe your story is not one of military violence or public scandal.
Maybe your battlefield is hidden.
A secret addiction.
An affair nobody knows about.
A bitterness you have carried for years.
A habit of lying to protect your image.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A hunger for money or recognition that has slowly taken the place of God.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are winning.
You have the job.
The income.
The influence.
The beautiful family photographs.
The appearance of stability.
But when the room becomes quiet, you know something is wrong.
You have learned to manage appearances while your soul grows exhausted.
And perhaps you have been telling yourself that because nothing terrible has happened yet, God must be approving of your choices.
But the delay of consequences is not proof of divine approval.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
His patience is mercy.
Not permission.
And there is a difference between God giving you time to repent and God endorsing the road you are traveling.
Please do not miss that.
The most frightening thing about Sisera's story is not merely that his mother did not know he was dead.
It is that his world had taught him to trust in a kind of power that could never save him.
Nine hundred iron chariots.
Twenty years of oppression.
A commander's authority.
A reputation built on fear.
And none of it could secure his life when the LORD brought judgment.
We build our own iron chariots today.
Money.
Status.
Connections.
Religious titles.
Public approval.
The number of people who applaud us.
The number of people afraid to confront us.
And we begin to believe those things make us untouchable.
But there is no human achievement powerful enough to cancel our need for repentance.
Jesus asks in Mark 8:36:
“For what doth it profit a man, to gain the whole world, and forfeit his life?” — ASV
What good is winning everyone's admiration if you are losing your soul?
What good is building a name that survives you if you have never surrendered to the Name above every name?
What good is being celebrated in a room full of people if you are running from the truth of God?
And what good is having people wait proudly for your return if the life you are living is leading you farther and farther from Christ?
These questions are not meant to drive you into hopelessness.
They are meant to awaken you while there is still time.
Because the story of Sisera is not the end of the Bible.
The Bible moves forward through Israel's failures, God's covenant promises, the cries of the prophets, and the longing for a Redeemer.
And eventually, it brings us to another scene of public shame and apparent defeat.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A wooden cross.
A suffering Savior.
Jesus Christ.
Unlike Sisera, Jesus did not build His mission on the oppression of the weak.
He came proclaiming good news to the poor, liberty to captives, and the kingdom of God.
He welcomed sinners without approving their sins.
He exposed hypocrisy without delighting in human humiliation.
He touched the unclean.
He defended the dignity of the vulnerable.
He called the proud to repentance.
And He willingly gave His life for sinners.
Isaiah 53:5 declares:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities; the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.” — ASV
At the cross, God did not pretend evil was harmless.
Sin was taken seriously.
Justice was not dismissed.
And mercy was revealed through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his own love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — ASV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we had cleaned up every secret.
Not after we had earned a second chance.
Not after we had finally become impressive enough to deserve God's attention.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to remain enslaved to the very sin from which Christ came to save us.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Grace teaches us to confess.
Grace changes the direction of our lives.
And grace reminds us that no amount of worldly success can compare with being reconciled to God.
The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament is μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It means to repent, involving a change of mind and heart that turns a person toward God.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what we did.
It is more than regretting the consequences.
It is turning from sin toward the Lord.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not merely to become a slightly improved version of your old self.
It is to receive new life through Jesus Christ.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Wherefore if any man is in Christ, he is a new creature: the old things are passed away; behold, they are become new.” — ASV
This is why we keep returning to the words that define Gospel Warrior:
Not because the past never happened.
Not because victims should be silenced.
Not because repentance eliminates every earthly consequence.
Not because forgiveness makes accountability unnecessary.
But because Jesus Christ can redeem sinners, restore what sin has broken according to His wisdom, and give a future that is no longer governed by rebellion against God.
His grace does not rewrite history by making evil good.
It rewrites the sinner's future through forgiveness, repentance, reconciliation with God, and transformation.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear.
You may not be able to change what happened yesterday.
You cannot undo every word you spoke.
You cannot recover every opportunity you wasted.
You cannot force every person you hurt to trust you again.
But you can come to Christ today.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can stop defending what God calls sin.
You can begin making things right where possible.
You can seek help.
You can surrender.
You can trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And if you are a parent waiting for a child who has wandered far from God, keep praying with love and truth.
Do not confuse unconditional love with unconditional approval.
Do not give up the truth to preserve temporary peace.
But do not give up on prayer either.
Speak the truth without cruelty.
Keep the door of honest reconciliation open where it is safe and appropriate.
Entrust what you cannot control to the Lord.
Your child's choices are not yours to make.
And your faithfulness cannot guarantee another person's repentance.
But you can bear witness to the grace of Christ.
And if you are the one who has wandered, hear this:
You do not have to wait until your life completely collapses before you return to God.
You do not have to wait for the iron chariots to fail.
You do not have to wait until the applause stops.
You do not have to wait until someone you love is standing at a window wondering what happened to you.
Come to Jesus now.
Not because you can promise Him a perfect tomorrow.
But because He is the risen Savior who receives repentant sinners.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — ASV
Stay with that conviction.
Bring it before God.
You do not have to publish your deepest sins to prove your repentance. Some confessions belong in private prayer, honest conversations, pastoral care, or appropriate accountability.
But perhaps you are ready to take one small, courageous step.
And if Christ has already begun restoring your life, share a word of testimony. Someone else may need to know that grace is not just a beautiful religious idea.
It is real.
It changes people.
It changes the way we love.
It changes the way we confront sin.
It changes the way we endure grief.
And it changes what we hope for when we look toward the road.
Maybe you know someone who needs this message.
A parent carrying a quiet burden.
A friend whose success is hiding spiritual exhaustion.
A believer who has slowly become comfortable with compromise.
A person who thinks they have gone too far for God's mercy.
Not merely to spread another post, but because someone in your circle may be wrestling with a question they have never dared to ask aloud.
There may come a day when you need to remember that God is not impressed by our chariots, our appearances, or our excuses.
He desires truth in the inward being, as Psalm 51:6 teaches.
He calls us to walk humbly with Him.
And He has given us Jesus Christ, the only Savior who can reconcile us to the Father.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, and even those who are still exploring the Christian faith to follow along.
Because discipleship should not stop with one emotional moment.
It should continue into the ordinary days when nobody is watching.
When temptation returns.
When prayer feels difficult.
When obedience costs something.
When the truth of Scripture must become more than words on a screen.
Our desire is to keep biblical resources accessible and to reach more people with the message of salvation, repentance, forgiveness, and transformation through Christ.
For some, it may be a meaningful part of their regular Christian giving.
But I want to be careful with something important.
The Bible teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that each person should give as they have purposed in their heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
For the believer who needs encouragement to return to Scripture.
For the parent praying over a wandering child.
For the person who has spent years believing that their past is too ugly for redemption.
For the soul that needs to hear the Gospel again.
You can pray for the ministry.
You can read and use the free resources.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not a product.
And the grace of God cannot be purchased.
Now, before you leave, I want you to picture that ancient window one more time.
The mother is still looking.
The road is still empty.
The women around her are still imagining the beautiful garments and the spoils of victory.
They do not know what has happened.
They do not know that the battle is over.
They do not know that the commander they are waiting for will never return.
And the silence grows heavier.
There is no triumphant arrival.
No victorious announcement.
No sound of chariot wheels.
Only the dreadful distance between what they expected and what was true.
Judges 5:31 ends with a prayer that the LORD's enemies would perish and that those who love Him would be like the sun rising in its strength.
It is a sober conclusion to a song of deliverance.
God had not forgotten His oppressed people.
Their cries had not been meaningless.
And the power that had terrified them for twenty years had not been greater than the LORD.
But for us, living on this side of the cross and resurrection, the story also directs our attention toward a greater and final hope.
We are not called to become proud spectators of another person's downfall.
We are called to repent, to trust Christ, to love truth, to defend the vulnerable, and to proclaim the mercy available through the risen Lord Jesus.
We do not know how Sisera's mother responded when she eventually learned the truth. Scripture does not tell us.
We should not invent her final words or pretend to know the eternal condition of her soul.
The Bible leaves her at the window.
And perhaps that unfinished image is part of what makes the passage so haunting.
Because the question is no longer merely what happened to her son.
The question is what we will do with the truth while we still have time to respond.
Will we keep defending the things God is exposing?
Will we keep trusting the chariots that cannot save us?
Will we keep calling success a blessing when it is built on someone else's suffering?
Or will we humble ourselves before Jesus Christ?
The One who does not merely offer a better appearance.
The One who gives new life.
The One who does not excuse sin but forgives repentant sinners.
The One who rose from the grave and calls us to follow Him.
If you have never surrendered your life to Christ, you can begin by turning to Him in honest faith and repentance.
Tell Him the truth.
Confess your need for His mercy.
Believe the Gospel of His death for our sins and His resurrection.
And begin walking with Him in the light of His Word, alongside a faithful Christian community.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have been hiding, come into the light.
If you have been waiting for someone, continue praying without surrendering truth.
And if you have been trusting in the wrong things, remember that the mercy of God is calling you to something better than a life built on fear, pride, and appearances.
One day, every earthly chariot will stop.
Every title will lose its power.
Every public applause will fall silent.
Every human life will stand before God.
But the hope of those who belong to Jesus Christ is not that they were strong enough to save themselves.
Their hope is that Christ died, Christ rose, and Christ is able to save those who come to God through Him.
So do not wait for everything you trust to collapse before you listen to the Savior calling you home.
Because the most heartbreaking thing is not always the empty road outside the window. Sometimes it is a heart so certain of its own victory that it never realizes how desperately it needs grace.
